title: Time & Work
shortDescription: Nobody is actually 'working for 10 days' in the math — you're measuring work rates. Once you see that, add the rates instead of averaging the times.
genZNote: Nobody is actually 'working for 10 days' in the question's math brain. We're measuring work rates. Once you see that, the question stops being scary.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: Treat the whole job as '1 unit of work'. A person who completes it alone in T days has a work RATE of 1/T (job per day). When multiple agents work together, their RATES add — never average the TIMES directly.

steps.name: Standard method (fractions)
steps.explanation: A finishes a job in 12 days, B in 18 days. Rate A = 1/12, Rate B = 1/18. Combined rate = 1/12+1/18 = 3/36+2/36 = 5/36. Time together = 36/5 = 7.2 days.

steps.name: Fast method — assume total work = LCM
steps.explanation: Let total work = LCM(12,18) = 36 units. A's rate = 36/12 = 3 units/day. B's rate = 36/18 = 2 units/day. Combined = 5 units/day. Time = 36/5 = 7.2 days.
steps.purpose: Whole-number 'units' are easier to add mentally than fractions — same answer, less fraction arithmetic.

sections.heading: Efficiency ↔ Time — the Inverse Relationship
sections.body: Efficiency and time taken are inversely related: if A is twice as efficient as B, A takes HALF the time B takes for the same job. When a question gives an efficiency ratio, convert it to a time ratio by inverting it (or vice versa) before combining with other information.

sections.heading: Pipes & Cisterns Variant
sections.body: An inlet pipe filling a tank has a positive rate; an outlet pipe draining it has a NEGATIVE rate. When pipes work together, subtract the draining pipe's rate rather than adding it — a very common sign error under time pressure.

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Averaging the two individual TIMES directly (e.g. (12+18)/2) instead of combining RATES — only rates add linearly for simultaneous work.
Forgetting to SUBTRACT (not add) an outlet pipe's rate when it works against inlet pipes.
Applying an efficiency ratio as a time ratio without inverting it first.

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: Assume total work = LCM of the given individual times — this converts fraction addition into whole-number addition, which is faster and less error-prone under time pressure.
Watch for 'drains' / 'empties' / 'leak' language — that's the signal to subtract a rate instead of adding it.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Work rate = 1/(time alone); combined rate is the sum of individual rates (subtracting for anything working against the group); time together = 1/(combined rate).
keyFacts: Rates add for simultaneous work; times never average directly.
Assume total work = LCM of given individual times to avoid fraction arithmetic.
Efficiency and time are inversely related — invert one to get the other.
An outlet/draining pipe's rate is subtracted, not added.
commonConfusion: Rates combine by addition; TIMES never do — averaging two completion times directly is always wrong.

highYieldFacts: Assuming total work = LCM of the given times converts the whole problem into whole-number 'units per day' arithmetic.
Efficiency ratio inverts to give the time ratio, and vice versa.
commonTraps: Averaging individual completion times instead of adding rates.
Adding an outlet pipe's rate instead of subtracting it.
mustRemember: Combined rate = sum of individual rates (subtract rates working against the group); time = 1/combined rate.
